label: explain2-bm-contract
one_line: Short answer: a printed, damp-bending shade probably cannot go on tall flats in England, and nobody we found pays for a design rule alone. So we offer a London design studio measurements, not promises.
what:
We want to offer a London design studio a small first sample. It is a printed strip made of two plastic layers. One layer swells in damp air and the other does not, so the strip curls. A curling strip could open or close a window shade with no motor.

We would also offer a design rule. The rule says how far a two-layer strip can possibly curl. It is simple: the curl can never be more than 1.5 times the size mismatch between the layers, divided by the strip's thickness. Think of a cheap oven thermostat. Its two metals grow by different amounts when warm, so the strip bends. Our strip does the same with damp instead of heat.

An old textbook formula already hints at this limit. A 2015 paper (Holstov) plotted it with numbers. What we add is a proof. We used a free maths-checking program called Lean. It is a theorem prover: software that checks a proof one tiny step at a time and refuses any gap. That means a person can trust the sums without redoing them. But Lean checks only the maths of a model. It does not show that a real printed strip will behave that way. That is why the sample must be measured.

Before building anything, eight research helpers read building rules, safety sheets, grant lists and patents. A patent is a legal right to an invention. This page sums up what they found about the contract side. It covers what the part must pass, what it costs to handle, who pays, and who owns what.

We do not know who "we" will be on the offer. We do not know if the team is a company or a university group. We also do not know what the sample will cost to make. The studio's making arm, called Fab.Pub, lists a minimum budget of 250 pounds (about the price of a good bicycle lock set) and no other fees. That is all we found.
why:
Many clever building ideas fail on boring questions. Will it burn? Is it safe to print? Who pays? Does someone already own the idea? Asking these first saves months of work.

It also stops us from saying things we cannot prove. Nobody has yet measured an energy saving from a damp-air shade. The best real example only measured how much shade it made. A fair offer should say that plainly. It should offer measurements the studio lacks, not big promises.

steps.text: Read the English building rules. Find out which parts of a tall building must be almost non-burning.
steps.picture: Checking the rulebook of a sport before you sign up a team.

steps.text: Check what burn data the printer maker publishes. Compare it with what the rules ask for. The maker gives only a small plastic burn test. The rules do not use it.
steps.picture: Asking whether your driving test covers the road you plan to use.

steps.text: Look for any test standard for parts that bend in damp air. We found none. So we note what researchers do instead.
steps.picture: Finding no recipe in any cookbook, so reading how other cooks improvised.

steps.text: Compare how much the two layers bend from heat and from damp. Both can curl the strip. Heat could hide the damp effect.
steps.picture: A metal thermostat strip that bends when warm, mixed up with a wet paper strip that curls.

steps.text: Read the safety sheets for the printing liquids and the waste rules. List what to avoid.
steps.picture: Reading the label on a strong glue before opening the tin.

steps.text: Search grant lists and the studio's own pages. See who pays for what, and when.
steps.picture: Reading a train timetable to see which trains run and which are cancelled.

steps.text: Scan patent records for ideas close to ours. Note which are still alive and which have ended.
steps.picture: Walking a fence line to see which plots are already claimed.

steps.text: Re-run the key sums and spot checks. A second set of readers rechecked the main claims.
steps.picture: Having a friend recount the change at a till.

wrong_if:
Before looking, we wrote down a bet. Nobody will pay for the design rule alone. And no printed resin will pass the fire rules for tall homes. A resin is a liquid plastic that hardens under light.

We would be wrong if a firm showed it pays for design rules alone. We would be wrong if a printed resin earned the top fire grade. We would also be wrong if someone measured a real energy saving from a damp-air shade. The helpers looked for all three and found none. But they could not search everywhere. So "we found none" is not the same as "none exists".
could_go_wrong: The helpers searched limited sources. So 'nobody has done this' may only mean 'we did not find it'.
The patent scan was only partly checked. The checkers could not open two key patent pages, so we leave those claims out.
The swelling figure for one bendy resin came from a scrambled data sheet. Nobody has re-measured it in damp air.
The strip may bend more from heat than from damp. That could hide the effect we want to show.
Grant lists change fast. Most European grants need an applicant based in Europe.
We do not know whether the team is a company or a university group. That decides which grants fit.
No patent lawyer has looked at anything. So who owns what is still open.
The studio prints with robot arms and plant-based plastic, not with resin or powder. So our samples only prove the shape idea, not a finished product.
Lean proves the maths of our model. It does not prove a printed strip will behave that way. Only measuring a real strip can show that.

questions.a: Each helper saved the pages it read and wrote down exact quotes. A second set of readers then rechecked the main claims. We only use claims they could confirm, in full or in part. The rest are listed under 'left out'.

We have not tested any printed strip yet. We did not read paid standards or the full text of some papers. We did not check Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland. No lawyer or fire engineer has reviewed this.

questions.q: Could a printed plastic part be used as a shade on a tall block of flats in England?
questions.a: Probably not. Take homes with a floor at 18 metres or higher. That is roughly six floors up. There, outer wall parts must be nearly non-burning. Shading slats are not exempt. Shading lower than 4.5 metres from the ground, about the height of a double-decker bus, falls outside that rule.

questions.q: Can we say the part is fire safe?
questions.a: No. A real fire grade needs large test pieces. A desk print is too small to be graded. The printer maker publishes only a small-scale plastic burn rating called UL 94. The English fire guide does not use it. The guide never mentions it.

Clients pay for finished installations. Public grants pay for early proof work. Window and shade makers join public projects but offer help, not cash. We found nobody who pays for a design rule alone. We may have missed some.

questions.q: Is the idea patented by someone else?
questions.a: Many nearby ideas are patented. So we cannot claim 'a plate that curls in damp air'. Some patents on wood versions are narrow. One live patent from MIT and a printer firm is the nearest to a resin-printed damp-swelling part. Its first and widest sentence is narrower than first thought. The first scan found no patent that pairs a computer-checked proof with print design. But a lawyer must confirm that.

With care, yes. All 14 resin sheets we checked mark the liquid as a skin allergy risk. That means repeated skin contact can cause a lasting allergy. Two resins also carry a warning for harm to unborn children or fertility. We would leave those out of any public sample. The washing liquid, rubbing alcohol, catches fire easily. So we need gloves, goggles and fresh air.

questions.q: Can we call it green or recyclable?
questions.a: No. The printer maker says cured resin and used powder cannot be recycled. It calls one powder partly plant-based but gives no percentage. New European Union rules limit vague claims like 'biobased' from 27 September 2026.

questions.q: Who is the team, and what does the studio get?
questions.a: We do not know yet whether the team is a company or a university group. The studio would get a small printed sample, measurements of how it curls, and the design rule with its proof. It would not get a finished building product.

questions.q: How much will the sample cost?
questions.a: We do not know. The studio's making arm lists only a minimum budget of 250 pounds and no other published fees.

questions.q: Why does the rule need a proof at all?
questions.a: An earlier paper plotted the same limit using numbers, but a plot is not a proof. A proof says no choice of layers can ever beat the limit. The program Lean checks that with no gaps. The limit applies to the maths model, so the real strip must still be measured.

glossary.plain: A small first sample built to show that an idea can work.
A strip made of two stuck-together layers.
To grow slightly bigger by soaking up water.
A liquid plastic that hardens under light when printed.
Fine plastic dust that a laser melts into a solid shape.
The name of one bendy printing resin made by Formlabs. It is the one whose swelling figure came from a scrambled data sheet.
A company that makes the 3D printers and materials we plan to use.
The name of one very stiff Formlabs printing resin. It takes up almost no water.
The name of one soft, rubbery Formlabs printing resin.
A tough plastic powder that the maker calls partly plant-based.
A material that changes shape when the air gets damper or drier. A pine cone is one.
A European grade for how fast a building material burns, from A1 (best) down.
A very high fire grade. The material barely burns, makes little smoke and drips no burning bits.
A small-scale test that rates how plastic burns in a thin sample. The building rules do not use it.
The English government guide on fire safety in buildings.
The English government guide on building materials and workmanship.
One floor of a building.
How much water vapour is in the air.
One full round of damp then dry, then back again.
A sealed box where heat and damp can be set and changed.
How much a material stretches or shrinks when its temperature changes.
Slow sagging of a material under steady load.
The slow wearing out of a material from sun, heat and time.
The official hazard page that comes with a chemical.
A chemical that can cause a lasting allergy after repeated skin contact.
A chemical that can harm unborn children or fertility.
A rubbing-alcohol liquid used to wash printed parts. It catches fire easily.
To seep out of a material into water.
A legal right that stops others copying a specific invention.
The first and usually widest sentence of a patent. It says what is protected.
Anything already public that can block a new patent.
A cheap early patent application that fixes a date.
Software that checks a maths proof one tiny step at a time. We used one called Lean.
The free theorem prover we used to check our curl limit.
Money given for research that does not have to be paid back.
Open for applications all year, with no single deadline.
A group of organisations that apply together for money.
The making arm of the London studio. It accepts material samples.
A UK scheme that pays for a university and a company to work together.
Small Business Innovation Research. US government awards for small firms, with a first phase and a larger second phase.
The Henry Royce Institute, a UK advanced-materials body. Its industry programme funds projects led by firms with universities.
A big US National Science Foundation grant for designing new materials. It runs only every second year.
Sloan is a US charity foundation. Holcim is a building-materials firm. Their grant pages could not be used.
An engineer who wrote the classic 1925 formula for how a two-layer strip bends.
The best mix of layer thickness and stiffness that makes the strip curl the most.
The thread-like root network of fungi. Some groups grow building panels from it.
Made at least partly from plants or other living sources.
A count of the environmental cost of a product from making to disposal.
The carbon dioxide released in making a material, before anyone uses it.
A 2024 test of 424 printed cellulose shade modules on a mock-up wall in Germany.
A number saying how much a material grows for each step up in damp.
A full-size trial model of part of a building.
A patent that has ended because fees were not paid or it was dropped.
The tough fibre found in plants and wood.
Ultraviolet light, the part of sunlight that fades and damages plastic.

check_yourself.what: Confirm the UK grant scheme named in the brief is closed.
check_yourself.expect: The text 'Smart grants are now closed for new applications'.

check_yourself.what: Check that the big US materials grant (DMREF) runs only every second year, and that the last window was early 2025.
check_yourself.expect: 'January 21, 2025 - February 04, 2025' and 'competitions biennially in odd-numbered years'.

check_yourself.what: Recompute the heat-versus-damp bending sums and the test-length sums.
check_yourself.expect: Difference in expansion 113.6 to 127.2 micrometres per metre per degree; thermal strain 0.454 % to 0.509 % over 40 K; 170 cycles = 1020 hours = 42.5 days (about six weeks).

check_yourself.what: Confirm the small-scale burn rating (UL 94) is absent from the English fire guide.
Check the swelling of the bendy resin in water by word position in the data sheet.
Re-run the humidity-versus-shade-need check for nine cities.
check_yourself.expect: Singapore 0.98 (shade mostly open in hours when shade is wanted), Madrid 0.95, Houston 0.38.

check_yourself.what: Re-run the Lean check of the curl limit, plus two deliberately false versions.
check_yourself.expect: 'errors=0 sorryAx=0' and 'ALL CHECKED', then Lean refusing the false 7/5 version with 'linarith failed to find a contradiction'.

left_out: US patent 11155025 B2 (MIT and Stratasys): its status and end date are unconfirmed. The checkers could not load the patent pages.
The claim that no patent pairs a theorem prover (a proof-checking program) with material or print design. The checkers could not reach the search pages.
The claim that an older patent text, citing the 1925 engineer Timoshenko, already gives the best layer mix. The page could not be fetched.
Whether the Sloan foundation and the building firm Holcim fund this kind of work. The checkers did not check.

'Smart grants closed, so three other routes are live.' Only the closure is confirmed. One agent's file says the first Knowledge Transfer round is closed. Eligibility for the Royce programme was not read.
'Only the Graham grant is open' among private funders. A second Graham grant (15 Nov 2026) is also open, so the claim is not safe.
'The only flexible resin that swells enough' and 'damp-air swelling numbers are unpublished'. The checkers did not confirm these.
'No standard exists' for damp-responsive parts, and 'only UL 94 is published'. These are claims that something is missing, which cannot be proved.
'Nine of 25 data sheets give a burn rating'. The count was not rechecked.
The 0.2 percent damp-swelling estimate. It is one agent's own guess and cannot be checked here.
'The only structural test on any practice page is one pull test'. This is wrong, because other pages report load tests.
'No energy or comfort benefit exists anywhere' for damp-driven shades. We say only that none was found.
'Mycelium has no verified fire grade.' The sources support only 'rarely tested'.
Claims about the studio's clients (Neko Health, COS, Buro Happold) and 'no fees published'. The checkers did not open these pages.
'No facade maker pays outsiders for material research' and the claim that Formlabs helps in kind. These negative findings were not checked.
changes: Rewrote one_line to open with the plain verdict: probably not for tall flats, nobody pays for a rule alone, offer measurements.
Added to 'what' who the offer is for, what the design rule is (curl never more than 1.5 times mismatch over thickness) and the thermostat comparison.
Added why a theorem prover is involved: it checks the proof with no gaps, but only proves the maths model, not the real strip. Credited the 2015 paper that plotted the limit.
Said plainly that we do not know who the team is (company or university) and do not know the sample cost; added the only cost fact, a 250 pound minimum at the studio's making arm.
Defined patent, resin and theorem prover where each first appears in the text.
Split the 'wrong_if' bet into short sentences and added that 'we found none' does not mean 'none exists'.
Rewrote the 'studio prints with robot arms' sentence and added a plain note that our samples prove only the shape idea.
Replaced 'claim 1', 'prior art' and 'provisional filing' in the answers with plain wording (first and widest sentence of a patent).
Explained UL 94 where it first appears in the fire answer, and Fab.Pub in 'what'.
Added comparisons: 4.5 metres as a double-decker bus, 42.5 days as about six weeks, 250 pounds as a bicycle lock set.
Defined skin allergy, harm to fertility and rubbing-alcohol washing liquid inside the safety answer.
Added three questions the reader could not answer: who the team is and what the studio gets, sample cost, why the rule needs a proof.
Added glossary entries for SBIR, Royce, DMREF, Sloan and Holcim, Timoshenko, bilayer ratio optimum and Lean; expanded hygromorph, consortium and embodied carbon.
Rewrote each 'left out' line that used jargon (claim 1, theorem prover, bilayer ratio optimum, Timoshenko, Sloan and Holcim) into plain sentences.
Added a Lean limits caution to could_go_wrong, a Lean re-run command to check_yourself, and the Holstov 2015 and Lean documentation sources.
Added a step 2 note that the maker's small burn test is not used by the rules, and step 4 note that heat can hide damp bending.
